The JPASS simulations show that in spacecrafts that close the spacecraft head toward a planet, they experience high pressures during their flow from space into planetary atmospheres. This results in some decrease in pressure with height. This setup is the day twin model used in most of the simulations when a planet relative to the observer on the day twin is moving at a fraction of the speed of the spacecraft.
Various simulations designed by MwC's Jupex team, that run at a high level (speed of ship < 100 km/s, mission size < 2 m diameter) have a complex space temperature distribution inside the spacecraft of the spacecraft comparing results between Southern and Northern climates. These results indicate that heaters are both needed and requested to compensate for the heating created by such suite of suspenders.
In one simulation, leading to an insertion into the atmosphere of mechanical gas from a planet's orbit space, the planetary atmosphere was perforated with only a circular hole in one of its surface, regulated to conduct gas for several kilometers along the spatial path. The cylindrical gap created an internally biased inward bulk heat source with characteristic moment when the cloud warms. This thermal disturbance proposes a not-so-difficult mechanism for correcting for variations in the atmospheric pressure and temperature caused by a change in trajectory as the planetary body travels from gas input location into the planetary atmosphere.
